extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in formal verification, automated theorem proving, and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and modeling what it takes for agents (humans or proof assistants) to understand and verify mathematical proofs; identifying strategies, representations, and structural features that make ordinary textbook inferences verifiable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory should provide causal explanation / mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: We expect a philosophical theory to provide some sort of causal explanation that tells us how intelligent and intentional behavior is brought about; a theory should explain how a proper understanding enables one to function mathematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that merely correlating behaviors with mental states 'tells the wrong kind of story.' A satisfactory theory should not only characterize outward signs of understanding but provide hypotheses or models (mechanisms) that explain the mental activity producing those behaviors. This is important for pedagogy and for guiding computer scientists who write software to exhibit competent mathematical behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account both outward criteria and internal mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: An ‘inner process’ stands in need of outward criteria; outward criteria are necessary and also sufficient to give our theoretical terms meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that while outward behavioral criteria are necessary to ascribe understanding, they can also be sufficient to give meaning to internal theoretical terms, provided we treat internal mechanisms as hypotheses or explanatory models (Wittgensteinian framing). A usable theory should bridge outward behavior and abstract abilities (e.g., 'recognize', 'determine', 'apply', 'recall').

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionalist description of subsystems and components
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of mathematical abilities should describe subsystems and components and how they interact, analogous to describing a car's subsystems for mechanical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends developing an appropriate language and conceptual framework to describe components of mathematical understanding (mechanisms at varying granularity). The framework should be guided by the data to be explained and the aims (pedagogical, computational) the explanations are to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model of proof must make 'seeing' nontrivial (support higher-level proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding textbook proofs involves being able to spell out details left implicit; therefore we need a model of proof on which 'seeing' such steps is a nontrivial affair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal axiomatic deduction (every detail spelled out) does not capture the higher-level steps mathematicians routinely take. The model should support representations (proof scripts) that correspond to higher-level methods and that the system (or theory) can treat as instructions for deriving an axiomatic proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof scripts as instructions / goal-driven proof style
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal 'proof scripts' can be viewed (like informal proofs) as providing instructions as to how to find a formal axiomatic derivation; proof assistants support a goal-driven style where each step reduces open goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper describes how systems like Coq, Isabelle, and HOL-light use goals/sequents and reduction steps (e.g., logical rules like and-introduction). A successful formal-verification workflow treats scripts as high-level procedures guiding the construction of detailed axiomatic derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying a step means constructing the corresponding formal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of proof assistants, 'understanding' a step means being able to justify the corresponding inference (i.e., produce or recognize the formal sequent proof A,B ⇒ E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even steps that are obvious to humans correspond to potentially hard sequents for the computer; the criterion highlights that formal justification—not merely informal plausibility—is the standard for 'understanding' in verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding combinatorial explosion from case splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive case distinctions (e.g., repeatedly splitting on disjunctions) can cause an exponential blowup in subgoals and must be managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 10 successive case splits yields 1024 subgoals. Effective proof-search and verification systems must include strategies (heuristics, delaying splits, contextual reasoning) to avoid infeasible branching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing term instantiation for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving existential conclusions or using universal hypotheses requires finding appropriate instances; there may be infinitely many terms and no a priori bound on how many are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search strategies should defer choosing explicit terms where possible (use Skolem functions) and rely on unification techniques to find useful instantiations. Effective systems delay commitments and employ heuristics to discover relevant terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and importing appropriate background theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifying common inferences usually requires background facts/theorems left implicit; the challenge is to determine which external facts to import into the local hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blindly importing large theories is intractable; systems need principled ways to identify relevant lemmas or facts (context management, libraries, relevance heuristics) so the local proof search remains tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward-driven search (backchaining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work backwards from the goal using rules that reduce the goal into subgoals (e.g., use x>y,y>0 ⇒ 1/x<1/y) — a common proof-search technique known as backchaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backchaining is natural but can lead to many alternative ways to justify a goal and thus to combinatorial case splits; systems must manage nondeterminism introduced by multiple backward decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-driven search (deriving useful facts in advance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work forwards from hypotheses to amass potentially useful inequalities/facts (e.g., noting positivity of terms) that can later be used to reduce backward search branching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward generation of invariants or lemmas is useful when facts will be reused. However, deriving facts blindly is unhelpful; choices must be driven by context and the goal to avoid explosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine specialized decision procedures (modular combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: More complex inferences can often be handled by combining methods from restricted domains (e.g., additive and multiplicative fragments), using principled combination frameworks like Nelson–Oppen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining 'local' decision procedures that are each tractable for a fragment can yield practical methods for richer theories. The criterion stresses modularity and principled communication between solvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heuristic procedures when decision procedures are infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic proof-search applies a battery of natural inferences systematically to find short justifications where full decision procedures are inefficient or infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision procedures (even when available, like Presburger/Tarski) may be too inefficient for practical proofs; heuristics and domain-specific inferences often produce much shorter, more practical justifications for the kinds of inferences found in textbook mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify structural features that enable principled methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful theory should identify structural features of mathematics that make principled and effective proof-search possible, rather than relying purely on ad-hoc heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author concedes some ad-hoc 'mucking around' in practice but urges seeking and formalizing the structural features (e.g., positivity, common patterns) that explain why particular heuristics succeed, thereby improving repeatability and mechanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support abstraction/instantiation in algebraic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic reasoning pivots on recognizing abstract structures (e.g., groups) and instantiating general theorems to particular domains; systems should support both abstraction and instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include generality, notational/terminological convenience, suppressing irrelevant details, and focusing investigation. Formal systems must make group-theoretic or other algebraic facts 'ready to hand' so that instantiation is natural and low-overhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide contexts/locales/modules where facts are 'ready to hand'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof assistants should provide mechanisms (contexts/locales/modules) that collect facts and procedures that are available for reasoning in a local scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Isabelle locales, Coq modules. The paper shows how locale-based lemmas (e.g., (in comm-group) power-order-eq-one) let one state and use algebraic theorems succinctly; such scoped contexts facilitate abstract reasoning and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent proofs at an appropriate level of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The language and representation of proofs should allow conveying algebraic/group-theoretic reasoning succinctly and in a way that mirrors informal mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Isabelle examples show that with appropriate locale/module support and notation, one can express results like Euler's theorem via a short chain of interpreted lemmas and simple rewriting steps, matching informal higher-level proofs while remaining checkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for decidability availability and practical efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when decision procedures (e.g., Presburger, Tarski) apply and exploit them, but also account for their computational inefficiency or infeasibility in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decision procedures where suitable, but prefer heuristics, modular combinations, or specialized algorithms when full decision methods are too slow or when the theory includes undecidable features (e.g., multiplication over integers, sin function over reals).
